doc.title: Sonny Igoe interviewed by Monk Rowe, Emerson, New Jersey, July 31, 2003

title: Teaching, CBS symphony and leaving studio work
summary: Igoe built a teaching practice, earned more than playing, dropped off the studio call list, and notes musician residuals.

story.theme_name: Radio and television work: staff jobs, shows and broadcasts
story.community_name: Studio work and jingles: New York session life

blocks.x: Well they had to cut down some men, yeah. I started teaching early in my career. I always liked to teach. And I have to say it myself because you don’t know but I’m good at it. I have the right disposition and the right patience and all that kind of stuff, and the right expertise. I’m very experienced. And I played with the CBS Symphony. I had a legitimate conductor at CBS who loved the way I played a roll. And he wanted me on everything that he did, because when there were rolls on the snare drum I was the guy. I couldn’t believe it. I couldn’t believe it. Everybody in the band would say that’s like the kiss of death, Sonny, if he likes you. So anyway that’s just another phase. But I did all that stuff. But I’m not by any means a concert percussionist. But I was exposed to all that. So my teaching involves a lot of stuff. And I have a lot of guys now, besides my son, I have three other guys working on Broadway who took lessons with me. And it’s good for my reputation as far as the teacher goes. But people don’t know me as a player anymore. And people really — not too many people heard me as a teacher anymore because it’s fading out. Not many people want to study. They don’t want to practice. The kids today they want to do a game and watch T.V. or something and play a game and have instant, unless someone is really gifted, they’re not going to practice. And I have a couple of good guys, but most of them are just floating along, something to do I guess, I don’t know. So when the stuff at CBS stopped in ’68 or almost ’69, I had already started to build up a teaching practice in New York. So I got into that very heavily. And I got to the point where I was making more money teaching than I ever made playing. So I said this is silly. So I had an answering service called Radio Registry which was the big place in New York. And they used to call me up and say, “Sonny, are you available such-and-

such for an hour?” And I’d say, “for an hour?” I said, “no I’m not available.” “Thank you, okay.” No an hour would mean I would have to bring my drum case in New York, probably put my car in at least two garages because I have to teach in the morning, then go record in the afternoon then go back and finish my teaching, and it winds up you’re not making any money. So that’s what happened to me. They finally called me one day about something and I said gee no, I can’t do it. She said, “are you working anymore? Do you want to work?” And I said, “to tell you the truth, why don’t you skip me for a while. I just want to see how I do with just the teaching.” And because we were in an era, there was a recession in the early 70s and everything instead of being two hours was an hour or instead of being four hours was two hours, and everything was getting cut back and all that kind of stuff. And the guys were really scrambling for dates. And there were a lot of dates but they didn’t pay as much. And the musicians didn’t share in residuals like the singers did. We got paid once around and then after that we got paid three-quarters, and then you got paid a half, then it went down to nothing practically. But the singers got paid big time. The best thing I ever had was once, the Olympics were in Japan, we did a Coca Cola commercial for four hours. That in itself was great. But then they brought the singers in and they did it in every conceivable language you could think so we got paid again for each one. It came to about $6000 or something like that, for four hours. I said boy I’d love to have a job like that all the time. But no go. So that was a long time ago, long time ago. Anyway.
